AI has the potential to enhance diagnostic precision, streamline clinical workflows, and facilitate disease detection before clinical manifestations become evident.

Methods

A narrative literature review was conducted to assess the impact of AI and machine learning in corneal disease preclinical diagnosis. A comprehensive search in PubMed was performed using key terms such as "artificial intelligence," "machine learning," "deep learning," "corneal diseases," and "early diagnosis." Eligible studies were those published in English over the last decade that focused on AI-driven diagnostic approaches and prognostic modeling. Case reports, nonoriginal studies, and those with minimal AI integration were excluded. Data extraction emphasized AI methodologies, imaging techniques, diagnostic performance metrics, and clinical relevance.

Results

AI-powered machine learning models analyze vast imaging datasets, detecting subclinical abnormalities imperceptible to conventional diagnostic methods. This capability is particularly significant in early keratoconus detection, dystrophies, infectious keratitis, conjunctival neoplasia, and other corneal pathologies such as dry eye or Steven-Johnson disease, where subtle morphological changes precede clinically apparent disease.

Conclusions

The integration of AI into corneal disease diagnostics and management could mark in the future a transformative shift in Ophthalmology, offering precision, efficiency, and scalability. By facilitating early disease detection and individualized patient assessments, AI minimizes diagnostic inconsistencies and accelerates clinical decision making. Continuous algorithm refinement and real-world validation are crucial to maximizing AI's clinical utility. To fully harness AI's potential, multidisciplinary collaboration among ophthalmologists, data scientists, and regulatory bodies is imperative to address standardization, ethical concerns, and implementation barriers. As AI-driven technologies continue to evolve, they will redefine the standard of care in corneal disease diagnosis, therapeutic precision, and patient outcomes.

records.title: The association between large language model dependence and academic anxiety among nursing students: statistical indirect associations through artificial intelligence addiction and academic burnout.

content.title: The association between large language model dependence and academic anxiety among nursing students: statistical indirect associations through artificial intelligence addiction and academic burnout.
content.abstract:
Background

Increasing use of large language models in nursing education has raised questions about the association between reliance on these tools and academic distress. This study examined direct and specific indirect associations between large language model dependence (LMD) and academic anxiety (AA) through artificial intelligence addiction (AIA) and academic burnout (AB).

Methods

A cross-sectional survey was conducted from March to April 2026 among 473 nursing students in Guangdong Province, China, including students undertaking clinical placements. The four constructs were assessed using items selected from published self-report instruments. Partial least squares structural equation modeling was performed with age and sex included as covariates. Direct and specific indirect associations were evaluated using bootstrapping with 5,000 resamples.

Results

Cronbach's α ranged from 0.914 to 0.944, composite reliability from 0.935 to 0.954, and average variance extracted from 0.560 to 0.721. Heterotrait-monotrait ratios ranged from 0.485 to 0.733, supporting discriminant validity. Model fit evidence was mixed: SRMR was 0.068, whereas NFI was 0.812, below the 0.90 reference value. The model explained 49.2% of the variance in academic anxiety. Large language model dependence showed a small positive direct association with academic anxiety (β = 0.138, 95% CI [0.006, 0.278], p = 0.048). Significant specific indirect associations were identified through academic burnout (β = 0.205, 95% CI [0.123, 0.303]) and through artificial intelligence addiction followed by academic burnout (β = 0.098, 95% CI [0.049, 0.147]); both p < 0.001.

Conclusion

Large language model dependence was positively associated with academic anxiety among nursing students, with specific indirect associations through academic burnout and through artificial intelligence addiction followed by academic burnout. These findings highlight the relevance of problematic AI use and study-related exhaustion to academic distress. However, the cross-sectional design does not establish temporal ordering or causal mediation.

records.title: Association between deep-learning-derived retinal aging speed and rapid decline of renal function in the Japanese general population.

content.title: Association between deep-learning-derived retinal aging speed and rapid decline of renal function in the Japanese general population.
content.abstract:
Background

The eye and the kidney share microvascular features, and retinal changes have been postulated to reflect systemic cardiometabolic dysfunction. Recently, retinal age, estimated by deep learning (DL) from a single fundus photograph, has been shown to predict cardiovascular events. The present study aimed to determine whether retinal aging speed, defined as the individual-specific annual rate of change in DL-estimated retinal age, is associated with rapid estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) decline.

Methods

We retrospectively analyzed the longitudinal data obtained from 7807 Japanese individuals who underwent repeated health check-ups with serial measurements of eGFR and fundus photographs (median 9.0 visits over median 8.0 years). We evaluated the relationship between retinal aging speed during the baseline period (from baseline to year 4) and rapid eGFR decline (≤ -3 ml/min/1.73 m²/year) during the follow-up period (after year 4).

Results

The incidence of rapid eGFR decline was significantly higher in the highest quartile of retinal aging speed than in the lowest quartile as the reference group in the fully adjusted model adjusting age, sex, body mass index, blood pressure, diabetes, smoking, eGFR, and proteinuria [odds ratio (OR) 1.34; 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.06-1.68; P = .015]. In the multivariable logistic regression models, retinal aging speed was associated with rapid eGFR decline after adjusting multiple key confounders (OR 1.14; 95% CI 1.02-1.29; P = .027).

Conclusions

Taken together, DL-derived retinal aging speed is independently associated with rapid eGFR decline in the Japanese general population.

records.title: Mapping Research on AI-Based Computer-Aided Diagnosis and Clinical Decision Support Systems: a Bibliometric Study Integrating Google Trends and Content Analysis.

content.title: Mapping Research on AI-Based Computer-Aided Diagnosis and Clinical Decision Support Systems: a Bibliometric Study Integrating Google Trends and Content Analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

Research on artificial intelligence-based computer-aided diagnosis and clinical decision support systems (AI-CDSS) is expanding, but integrated evidence on publication patterns, keyword trajectories, online search activity, and methodological characteristics remains limited.

Objective

To characterize AI-CDSS research by integrating bibliometric analysis, Google Trends comparison, and structured content analysis of citation-ranked publications.

Methods

Scholarly interest was assessed using bibliometric analysis of Web of Science records from 2016 through August 2026, including author-keyword co-occurrence, bibliographic coupling, and reference co-citation, whereas Google Trends was used to characterize online search activity. A structured content analysis of citation-ranked publications was conducted to examine applications, methodological characteristics, and reported limitations.

Results

We analyzed 19,809 included publications from 2016 through August 2026. Output rose approximately 21-fold, from 193 records in 2016 to 4,082 in 2025. Output was geographically concentrated within the included corpus, with a Gini coefficient of 0.869. Among records with identifiable corresponding-author country or territory, China, the United States, and India accounted for 61.33%. Scientific Reports was the most frequent source (n = 916). Frequent artificial intelligence- and diagnosis-related keywords included machine learning (n = 5,666), deep learning (n = 4,022), and computer-aided diagnosis (n = 1,512). Bibliographic coupling identified 15 publication communities, and reference co-citation identified seven reference communities. In the monthly level-series comparison, 9 of 10 keyword concepts exhibited significant associations with Google Trends relative search interest, but none of the 10 first-difference associations remained significant after Bonferroni adjustment. Content analysis of 215 citation-ranked publications, including 191 empirical publications, showed frequent use of convolutional neural networks in diagnostic and radiology applications. Common limitations included limited external validation, infrequent calibration reporting, and sparse workflow-level or impact evaluation.

Conclusion

AI-CDSS research has rapidly expanded around machine learning, deep learning, and diagnostic applications, but the analyzed citation-ranked publications provide more evidence of methodological development than of clinical deployment. Integrating bibliometric, search-activity, and content-based perspectives shows limited short-term correspondence between online search activity and scholarly keyword use and highlights the need to move beyond model development toward independent external validation, prospective workflow and patient-outcome evaluation, calibration, fairness, and postdeployment monitoring.

records.title: Application of an Artificial Intelligence Simulated Patient Model in Teaching Neurosurgical Decision-Making.

content.title: Application of an Artificial Intelligence Simulated Patient Model in Teaching Neurosurgical Decision-Making.
content.abstract:
Aim

Training in neurosurgical decision-making remains a challenging component of standardized residency training. Traditional teaching models are limited in their ability to simulate the uncertainty and complexity encountered in real-world clinical scenarios. As a novel educational tool, the potential value of artificial intelligence (AI)-simulated patient models in surgical decision-making training requires further evaluation. This study aimed to explore the application of an AI-simulated patient model in neurosurgical decision-making education and to assess its effectiveness in improving residents' clinical decision-making abilities.

Methods

A retrospective study was conducted involving 157 residents who underwent standardized residency training in the Department of Neurosurgery from January 2023 to April 2026. Based on the implementation of the AI-simulated teaching model beginning in January 2025, participants were divided into two groups according to the teaching model used: an experimental group (n = 72, receiving AI-simulated patient teaching from January 2025 to April 2026) and a control group (n = 85, receiving traditional case discussion teaching from January 2023 to December 2024). The experimental group used a large language model-based virtual patient system powered by DeepSeek to perform dialogue-driven history taking, image interpretation, surgical planning, and risk prediction with real-time feedback, while the control group received conventional methods. After teaching, an objective structured clinical examination (OSCE) was used to assess surgical decision-making across five dimensions, including localization diagnosis, surgical approach, risk identification, emergency management, and surgical timing, and a questionnaire was used to measure teaching satisfaction.

Results

The total score for surgical decision-making ability was significantly higher in the experimental group than in the control group (p < 0.001). Dimensional analysis showed that localization diagnosis, surgical method selection, risk identification, emergency response, and surgical timing judgment were higher in the experimental group than in the control group (all p < 0.05). The excellent rate for each assessment dimension (>85 points) was significantly higher in the experimental group than in the control group (p < 0.05). The satisfaction score was also higher in the experimental group than in the control group (p < 0.001).

Conclusions

The AI-simulated patient model based on a general-purpose large language model was associated with better surgical decision-making performance among neurosurgery residents. It has significant advantages in localization diagnosis, surgical approach selection, risk identification, emergency response, and judgment of surgical timing, and is well accepted by residents.

records.title: Beyond scales: Artificial intelligence, language, and behavior in suicide risk modeling-a narrative review.
records.publisher: European neuropsychopharmacology : the journal of the European College of Neuropsychopharmacology

content.title: Beyond scales: Artificial intelligence, language, and behavior in suicide risk modeling-a narrative review.
content.abstract: Suicide is a leading, preventable cause of premature mortality, yet identifying individuals at imminent risk remains difficult. There are no validated biomarkers for routine stratification, and common approaches (clinical interviews, rating scales, self-report) are limited by subjectivity, reporting bias, and weak positive predictive value for rare outcomes. Rapid advances in artificial intelligence (AI)-including machine learning, deep learning, and large language models-offer opportunities to integrate heterogeneous signals relevant to risk and treatment response. This narrative review summarizes recent AI-enabled prediction and characterization of suicidal thoughts and behaviors across major data modalities: structured electronic health records and claims; natural language processing of clinical notes and digital text; speech and facial/behavioral signals; neuroimaging and other neurobiological measures; and passive sensing from smartphones and wearables. We review common modeling and evaluation practices, emphasizing clinically relevant performance assessment (discrimination and calibration) and the importance of temporal and external validation. We also highlight barriers to translation, including class imbalance and label noise, dataset shift across sites and time, limited prospective evaluation, and the need for interpretable outputs that can support medication decisions and care pathways (e.g., triage, monitoring, and stepped interventions). Ethical and implementation challenges-privacy and consent, algorithmic bias and equity, governance, and the clinical consequences of false-positive and false-negative predictions-are discussed with an emphasis on safe deployment. We conclude with priorities for the field, including multimodal longitudinal cohorts, harmonized reporting standards, and pragmatic trials to determine whether AI decision support measurably improves suicide-prevention outcomes.

records.title: Global research trends of artificial intelligence in echocardiography (1984-2025): a bibliometric analysis.

content.title: Global research trends of artificial intelligence in echocardiography (1984-2025): a bibliometric analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

Echocardiography has evolved substantially since its introduction in 1954. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers transformative potential for image acquisition, quantification, interpretation, and reporting. Despite growing research interest, a comprehensive evaluation of the historical trends and evolution of AI in echocardiography is lacking. The study aimed to conduct a comprehensive bibliometric analysis of the global research landscape in this field.

Methods

A systematic literature search was conducted using the Scopus and Web of Science Core Collection databases for publications on AI in echocardiography from inception through November 10, 2025; no language filter was applied. Data analysis was performed using Microsoft Excel, Microsoft Access, and IBM SPSS Statistics. In addition, bibliometric mapping and data visualization were conducted.

Results

Overall, 2682 publications received 35,083 citations (mean, 13.08 citations per publication), spanning 1984-2025. Original articles, conference papers, and review articles accounted for 87.4% and 98.5% of total publications and citations, respectively. Publication output remained limited until approximately 2015, rose gradually thereafter, and accelerated markedly after 2018, with similar output in 2024 and 2025. The United States led in both publication volume and total citations, followed by China and the United Kingdom. The United States also had the highest collaboration link strength, and seven of the top 10 institutions were in North America (six in the United States and one in Canada). Mayo Clinic ranked first, with 142 publications and 3604 citations, and had the earliest first indexed publication among the top institutions (1992). The journal JACC: Cardiovascular Imaging ranked first in both total citations (1,911) and citations per publication (36.75). "Echocardiography," "deep learning," "artificial intelligence," and "machine learning" were the most frequently used terms. The thematic evolution showed continuity of algorithmic-centric themes (1984-2019) with emerging clinically oriented themes (2020-2025).

Conclusions

This comprehensive bibliometric analysis highlights the rapid expansion of AI research in echocardiography, characterized by an accelerating publication output and emerging clinically oriented research topics. These findings reflect growing research interest in integrating AI into echocardiographic practice and highlight the need for future research prioritizing multicenter validation, clinical translation, and equitable real-world implementation.

records.title: Artificial Intelligence in Corneal Refractive Surgery: A Bibliometric Analysis of Research Hotspots, Development Trends, and Emerging Directions

content.title: Artificial Intelligence in Corneal Refractive Surgery: A Bibliometric Analysis of Research Hotspots, Development Trends, and Emerging Directions
content.abstract: Purpose To characterize the research landscape, major hotspots, and evolving trends in artificial intelligence (AI) applications in corneal refractive surgery and to examine how these applications differ across surgical procedures. Methods English-language Articles and Reviews published between January 2018 and July 12, 2026 were identified from the Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC). VOSviewer and CiteSpace were used to examine publication trends, countries, institutions, authors, keywords, thematic clusters, temporal patterns, and citation bursts. AI applications were then compared across SMILE, LASIK/FS-LASIK, and PRK/TransPRK. Results The analysis included 79 publications. Publication activity increased after 2022 and reached its highest level in 2026. China and the United States were prominent contributors and occupied central positions in the international collaboration network. Major research themes included artificial intelligence, deep learning, machine learning, LASIK, SMILE, corneal imaging, and keratoconus. Over time, the research focus moved from refractive surgery safety assessment toward AI-assisted analysis and imaging applications. Across LASIK, SMILE, and PRK, AI research mainly addressed corneal parameter assessment, surgical evaluation, and prediction of postoperative outcomes. Conclusions AI research in corneal refractive surgery has expanded considerably in recent years, with increasing emphasis on deep learning, machine learning, and corneal imaging. Current studies mainly concern LASIK, SMILE, and PRK, covering preoperative assessment, corneal parameter analysis, and postoperative outcome prediction. The present bibliometric analysis maps the main research directions and their development over time and may help identify areas for further investigation and clinical translation.

records.title: Automated assessment of healthcare de-escalation communication skills in a conversational AI virtual reality simulation.

content.title: Automated assessment of healthcare de-escalation communication skills in a conversational AI virtual reality simulation.
content.abstract:
Introduction

Digital health training environments increasingly require scalable methods for assessing communication skills in realistic, interactive scenarios. This paper presents a comparative study of automated assessment approaches within a conversational AI virtual reality simulation designed for verbal de-escalation training.

Methods

A total of 20 nursing students completed the simulation, where their spoken responses were captured and converted to text through a speech-to-text system, and were evaluated across 11 de-escalation competencies. The evaluation compared three fine-tuned deep learning models (BERT, RoBERTa, and XLNet) with a modified RATAS, a rubric-driven framework that leverages large language models. Two experiments were conducted: one using controlled 100-item validation datasets for each section, and another using the real-world responses collected during the user study.

Results

On the validation datasets, the deep learning models achieved the highest performance, with RoBERTa obtaining an average accuracy of 0.9927, followed by BERT at 0.9900 and XLNet at 0.9790, while RATAS achieved 0.8554. On the student-response dataset, performance decreased for all approaches, with RoBERTa obtaining 0.8590 accuracy, RATAS 0.8181, BERT 0.8000, and XLNet 0.7681.

Discussion

These results suggest that transformer-based models perform best under controlled conditions, whereas RATAS demonstrated stability in grading across different dataset types. These preliminary findings support the feasibility of integrating deep learning and rubric-driven LLM-based automated assessment approaches for communication and de-escalation training in nursing education.

records.title: Impact of Image Bit Depth Reduction on Deep Learning Performance in Chest Radiograph Analysis: A Multi-institutional Study.

content.title: Impact of Image Bit Depth Reduction on Deep Learning Performance in Chest Radiograph Analysis: A Multi-institutional Study.
content.abstract:
Rationale and objectives

Medical imaging typically generates 12-bit to 16-bit formats, yet conversion to 8-bit is often required. While deep learning has been widely explored in medical imaging, the influence of image bit depth on model performance is not fully understood. This study evaluates the impact of conversion from 16-bit to 8-bit for sex, age, and obesity classification using deep learning.

Materials and methods

In this retrospective, multi-institutional study, we analyzed 100,002 chest radiographs from 48,047 participants across three institutions. Images were uniformly quantized from the fixed 0-65535 range to 256 levels (0-255) with no additional processing. Three convolutional neural network architectures (ResNet52, EfficientNetB2, and ConvNeXtSmall) were trained on both 16-bit and 8-bit versions of the images. Model performance was evaluated using internal test datasets, randomly split multiple times, and an external test dataset. Statistical analysis included paired comparisons of area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC) values, with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons.

Results

Across all architectures and classification tasks, differences between 16-bit and 8-bit model performance were minimal (mean differences ranging from -0.218%-0.184%). Statistical analyses revealed no significant differences in AUC-ROC values between bit depths for any model-task combination (all p values > 0.05 after Bonferroni correction). Effect sizes were small to moderate (Cohen's d ranging from -0.415-0.391).

Conclusion

No statistically significant differences were detected between models trained on 16-bit and 8-bit images in the three evaluated tasks. These findings suggest that conversion to 8-bit images may reduce data storage requirements and improve data processing efficiency. Further research is needed to assess their usefulness in clinical tasks.

records.title: Artificial Intelligence in Breast Cancer Diagnosis, Treatment, and Perioperative Management: A Systematic Review of Current Applications and Future Perspectives.

content.title: Artificial Intelligence in Breast Cancer Diagnosis, Treatment, and Perioperative Management: A Systematic Review of Current Applications and Future Perspectives.
content.abstract:
Background

Breast cancer is the most frequently diagnosed malignancy in women globally, accounting for approximately 2.30 million new cases and 666,103 deaths in 2022. Artificial intelligence technologies including machine learning, deep learning, radiomics, and natural language processing have been widely applied across the breast cancer care continuum. However, no systematic review restricted to primary studies with patient-level or image-level data has synthesized evidence spanning all clinical domains simultaneously.

Objectives

To evaluate the performance, methodological quality, and clinical relevance of artificial intelligence primary studies across screening and diagnostic imaging, digital pathology, radiomics, perioperative management, prognostic prediction, and natural language processing in breast cancer.

Methods

PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched from January 2015 to May 2026. Eligibility was restricted to original primary research reporting patient-level or image-level data; secondary syntheses were explicitly excluded. Risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-2 and PROBAST. Reporting followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines.

Results

Of 5,275 identified records, 17 primary studies met eligibility criteria. In screening mammography (seven studies; n = 7,540 to 144,231 examinations), deep learning achieved area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) values of 0.876 to 0.939; a randomised trial in 80,033 women demonstrated non-inferiority to double reading with a 44.3% reduction in radiologist workload. In digital pathology (five studies; 270 to 44,732 whole-slide images), deep learning achieved AUC 0.985 to 0.994, exceeding unassisted pathologist performance in lymph node metastasis detection. Magnetic resonance imaging radiomics predicted pathological complete response in HER2-positive breast cancer with AUC 0.80. No breast cancer-specific perioperative primary study met the eligibility criteria. Deep survival networks achieved concordance index 0.626 versus 0.612 for Cox regression in breast cancer cohorts. Natural language processing identified metastatic recurrence in breast cancer clinical records with sensitivity 83% and specificity 73%. Risk of bias was low to moderate for imaging and pathology studies and high for small sample radiomics studies. Density-stratified performance was reported by only two imaging studies, and receptor status prediction from haematoxylin and eosin staining had not been validated as a safe alternative to immunohistochemistry.

Conclusions

Artificial intelligence demonstrated clinically meaningful performance across the five domains with eligible primary studies. Breast cancer-specific perioperative and intensive care primary studies were absent, representing the largest evidence gap. External validation, demographic diversity, and prospective clinical integration evidence remained the most consistently identified limitations. Prediction of molecular receptor status without immunohistochemistry requires rigorous prospective safety validation before it can complement standard testing.

records.title: Digital twin oncology and multi-omics-driven artificial intelligence models for personalized drug response prediction: A systematic survey of emerging computational paradigms and clinical implementation challenges.

content.title: Digital twin oncology and multi-omics-driven artificial intelligence models for personalized drug response prediction: A systematic survey of emerging computational paradigms and clinical implementation challenges.
content.abstract: The increasing complexity of tumor heterogeneity and variable therapeutic response has intensified the need for accurate personalized drug response prediction in oncology. Traditional trial-and-error chemotherapy strategies often result in suboptimal outcomes, toxicity, and delayed therapeutic adjustments. Rapid advances in multi-omics technologies, artificial intelligence (AI) and digital twin modeling have significantly reshaped computational oncology research. This survey systematically reviews peer-reviewed research and review articles published from 2021 onward that investigate emerging computational paradigms integrating digital twins and multi-omics AI for drug response prediction. The foundational concepts in digital twin oncology, multi-omics profiling and AI-driven precision medicine are outlined initially. The existing approaches are categorized into four major paradigms such as omics-driven machine learning models, deep learning based multimodal architectures, mechanistic digital twin simulation frameworks and hybrid digital twin AI systems enabling adaptive therapy optimization. The multi-omics data integration strategies, including early, intermediate, late, network-based and graph/pathway-based fusion techniques. The survey synthesizes recent developments in drug sensitivity prediction, immunotherapy response modeling, tumor evolution forecasting and virtual clinical trials, while critically analyzing challenges related to data heterogeneity, interpretability, generalization, privacy, regulatory compliance and ethical considerations. Finally, future directions are highlighted such as real-time adaptive digital twins, federated learning, explainable AI and regulatory ready clinical deployment frameworks. Overall, this review provides a structured taxonomy, comparative analysis and research roadmap for advancing integrated digital twin and multi omics AI systems toward clinically actionable precision oncology.

records.title: Is Large Language Model a New Hope for the Global South? A Rapid Bibliometric Synthesis of Artificial Intelligence in Anatomy Education.

content.title: Is Large Language Model a New Hope for the Global South? A Rapid Bibliometric Synthesis of Artificial Intelligence in Anatomy Education.
content.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), especially the recent proliferation of generative Large Language Models (LLMs), is transforming traditional anatomy education by introducing new teaching tools. However, the adoption of these cutting-edge technologies raises questions about global educational equity. It remains unclear whether AI will serve as a digital equalizer or further exacerbate marginalization. This rapid bibliometric synthesis aims to provide a comprehensive, data-driven overview of the "Application of Artificial Intelligence in Anatomy Education" (AAAE). We seek to map the intellectual landscape, detect structural and technological shifts, evaluate the geopolitical disparities, and provide corresponding references. A total of 85 consolidated records were retrieved from Web of Science and Scopus. These data constituted the whole panorama of AAAE. Bibliometrix and CiteSpace were utilized for static and dynamic mapping. A multidisciplinary expert panel validated the thematic clusters using Gwet's AC1 and the Normalized Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI). Publications surged following ChatGPT's release, indicating a shift from specialized computer vision to the application of general-purpose LLMs. While high-income countries maintain leadership, AI could exert a "democratizing effect" on upper-middle-income countries, doubling their odds of publication compared to traditional anatomy. Six research frontiers and three research trajectories were captured, and corresponding implications for future researchers in the global south and north were presented. AAAE could be conducted using a stratified strategy: different expansions of AI technologies for pedagogy; leveraging commercial APIs to bypass infrastructure bottlenecks; and validating open-source models. Global equity critically demands cross-border collaboration and inclusive datasets.

records.title: Artificial intelligence analysis of oral mucosal lesions in white-light clinical photographs: A systematic review of visual features and validation.

content.title: Artificial intelligence analysis of oral mucosal lesions in white-light clinical photographs: A systematic review of visual features and validation.
content.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to conventional oral photographs for recognition, classification, localization, segmentation, and risk assessment of oral mucosal lesions. This systematic review evaluated how clinically relevant visual information-including color, texture, morphology, borders, and spatial patterns-is represented by AI systems and assessed performance, validation, explainability, human comparison, and clinical translation. PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Google Scholar were searched for studies directly analyzing conventional white-light clinical photographs. Risk of bias was assessed with PROBAST + AI, and certainty with Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation-based approaches. Fifty-three studies were included, 30 published in 2025-2026. Forty-six used implicit deep-learning visual representations, three multimodal vision-language models, two explicit color analyses, and two explicit texture analyses. Thirty-one studies primarily addressed image-level diagnostic classification/recognition, 15 spatial detection/localization or lesion delineation, six screening/triage/referral or biopsy-oriented decision support, and one longitudinal malignant-transformation prediction. Six used independent external cohorts and five compared AI with human readers. Methodological concerns were frequent, no sufficiently coherent group supported meta-analysis, and certainty remained limited across evidence bodies. Current evidence therefore supports technical feasibility rather than established clinical effectiveness, with translation requiring stronger patient-level independence, external validation, prospective multicenter evaluation, and evidence of clinical benefit.

records.title: Applications of Artificial Intelligence-Driven Chatbots in University Level Dental Education: A Systematic Review.

content.title: Applications of Artificial Intelligence-Driven Chatbots in University Level Dental Education: A Systematic Review.
content.abstract:
Background

Artificial intelligence (AI), mainly AI-driven chatbots and large language models (LLMs) is reshaping dental education through adaptive, interactive, and simulation-based learning. While the transition in technology has been rapid, the evidence about the educational effectiveness of these technologies is still very diverse and not entirely directed.

Aim

To analyze the roles, educational effectiveness, and impact of integrating AI-driven chatbots and LLMs in dental education at the university level with a focus on learning outcomes and implementation practices.

Methods

The researchers conducted a thorough search of the electronic databases PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Embase for articles published from January 2018 to November 2025. This review met the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 criteria and was made up of original research articles on dental studentsand educators who were using AI-based chatbots as interventions. The outcomes measured were knowledge gain, clinical reasoning, diagnostic accuracy, communication skills, and engagement of learners. Due to the differences in the methodologies used the authors opted for a narrative synthesis approach.

Results

Six studies met the eligibility criteria and showed potential benefits of AI-driven chatbots and LLMs for diagnostic reasoning, learning performance, engagement, and individualized feedback although methodological and outcome heterogeneity limited direct comparison.

Conclusion

AI-driven chatbots and LLMs may complement university-level dental education, but their effectiveness and safe implementation require further rigorous evaluation.

records.title: Impact of Prompt Formulation and Case Complexity on Large Language Model Performance in Otolaryngology.
records.publisher: Otolaryngology--head and neck surgery : official journal of American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery

content.title: Impact of Prompt Formulation and Case Complexity on Large Language Model Performance in Otolaryngology.
content.abstract:
Objective

To assess how prompt formulation and clinical complexity influence the performance of large language models (LLMs) in real otolaryngology cases.

Study design

Comparative observational study.

Setting

University hospital study.

Methods

Clinical information from 80 consecutive outpatients prospectively recruited at two otolaryngology centers and from 40 published case reports was submitted to ChatGPT-5, Claude-Sonnet-4.5, and Gemini-2.5-Pro using two prompt strategies: a physician-oriented prompt with medical terminology, and a patient-oriented prompt using lay language. Cases were classified by two board-certified otolaryngologists as simple, moderate, or complex (case reports). LLM responses were rated by two otolaryngologists using the Artificial Intelligence Performance Instrument (AIPI), with adequate inter-rater reliability (intraclass correlation coefficient [ICC] = 0.855) on a subset of complex, practitioner-prompt cases, and performance was analyzed according to prompt formulation and case complexity.

Results

Claude-Sonnet-4.5 and Gemini-2.5-Pro significantly outperformed ChatGPT-5 across differential diagnosis, additional examinations, treatment sub-scores, and total AIPI score (P < .001). Prompt origin significantly influenced performance: patient prompts yielded lower accuracy than practitioner prompts for medical history, symptoms, and primary diagnosis (P < .001). LLMs performed better on simple cases for history consideration, but on moderate-to-complex cases for physical examination, differential diagnoses, and additional examinations. Primary diagnostic accuracy peaked for moderate cases (54.6%) and dropped for complex ones (28.7%; P < .001).

Conclusion

LLM performance is significantly influenced by prompt formulation and clinical complexity, highlighting the importance of structured prompts and supervised clinical use. These findings suggest that the accuracy and clinical relevance of LLM outputs must be interpreted considering both prompt formulation and the amount of clinical information available to the model-a critical consideration for future integration of these tools into clinical practice.

records.title: Artificial Intelligence for Brain MRI Diagnosis: A Scoping Review and Evidence-Gap Map Across Neurological Diseases.

content.title: Artificial Intelligence for Brain MRI Diagnosis: A Scoping Review and Evidence-Gap Map Across Neurological Diseases.
content.abstract:
Introduction/objective

Artificial Intelligence (AI), including machine learning and deep learning, is increasingly applied to brain Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) for disease detection, classification, segmentation, and clinically relevant prediction. This review aimed to map the evidence on AI-assisted brain MRI diagnosis, identify methodological and clinical translation gaps, and propose priorities for future research.

Methods

This scoping review was conducted according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and Web of Science were searched for peer-reviewed English-language publications from January 2018 to April 2026. Data were charted according to disease domain, study design, AI method, dataset, validation strategy, performance metrics, explainability, and key limitations.

Results

The search identified 1,020 records. After duplicate removal and screening, 61 publications were included, comprising 24 original studies used for the primary evidence map and 37 reviews or commentaries used for contextual synthesis. Evidence was strongest for brain tumor imaging and Alzheimer's disease, whereas stroke, multiple sclerosis, pediatric neuroimaging, and rare neurological conditions were underrepresented. Most studies relied on public benchmark datasets and retrospective validation, whereas external validation, prospective clinical evaluation, subgroup analysis, explainability, and workflow integration were inconsistently reported.

Discussion

The findings indicate that AI-assisted brain MRI research remains unevenly developed and is constrained by dataset dependence, limited external validation, limited prospective clinical evaluation, and inconsistent reporting of explainability, subgroup performance, and workflow integration.

Conclusion

AI shows promising research-stage potential for brain MRI-based diagnosis, particularly in brain tumor analysis and Alzheimer's disease classification. Future research should prioritize multicenter validation, diverse and disease-specific datasets, explainable and equitable AI design, transparent reporting, and prospective evaluation within real clinical workflows.

records.title: Comparison of the efficacy of different orthotopic neobladder reconstruction techniques following radical cystectomy for bladder cancer: a network meta-analysis.

content.title: Comparison of the efficacy of different orthotopic neobladder reconstruction techniques following radical cystectomy for bladder cancer: a network meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

Orthotopic neobladder (ONB) reconstruction is increasingly utilized following radical cystectomy (RC) for bladder cancer (BC). However, the comparative functional performance of different ONB techniques remains inconclusive.

Materials and methods

A systematic review and network meta-analysis were conducted in accordance with the PRISMA-NMA guidelines. The study protocol was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251143294). PubMed, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Library were systematically searched from database inception to October 2025. Eligible studies included those enrolled patients undergoing RC with any ONB technique and reported at least one predefined outcome: maximum neobladder capacity (MNC), maximal flow rate (MFR), postvoid residual volume (PVR), daytime continence (DC), or nighttime continence (NC). A Bayesian random-effects model was applied to synthesize direct and indirect evidence and to rank interventions using the surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA).

Results

Fifteen studies involving 1,129 patients and 14 ONB reconstruction techniques were included. Most techniques showed no statistically significant differences compared with the Studer pouch across core functional outcomes. However, the Studer pouch demonstrated superior DC compared with the Camey I pouch, while the ileocecal pouch achieved significantly lower PVR than the Studer pouch (both P < 0.05). SUCRA-based rankings indicated that the T pouch, Xing pouch, Ileocecal pouch, Y pouch, and Mainz pouch performed best for MNC, MFR, PVR, DC, and NC, respectively.

Conclusion

Across five core functional outcomes, most ONB reconstruction techniques demonstrated comparable performance. SUCRA-derived rankings may facilitate individualized selection of ONB reconstruction techniques in clinical practice.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251143294, identifier CRD420251143294.

records.title: Artificial intelligence, extended reality and computational modelling in cross-sectional cardiovascular imaging in congenital heart disease: a narrative review.

content.title: Artificial intelligence, extended reality and computational modelling in cross-sectional cardiovascular imaging in congenital heart disease: a narrative review.
content.abstract:
Background and objective

Artificial intelligence (AI), extended reality (XR), and computational modelling are increasingly integrated with cross-sectional cardiovascular imaging, particularly computed tomography (CT) and cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR), to address the diagnostic and therapeutic complexity of congenital heart disease (CHD). Given the lifelong and heterogeneous nature of CHD, these technologies have the potential to enhance anatomical assessment, haemodynamic understanding, procedural planning, and personalised care. This narrative review aims to provide a structured overview of current developments, clinical applications, and translational challenges related to AI, XR, and computational modelling in CT- and CMR-based CHD imaging.

Methods

A targeted literature search was performed in PubMed to identify representative and clinically relevant publications from January 2014 to October 2025, including early online articles. Search terms included combinations of "artificial intelligence", "deep learning", "extended reality", "virtual reality", "computational modelling", "computational fluid dynamics", "3D printing", "congenital heart disease", "cardiovascular magnetic resonance", and "computed tomography". English-language original articles, reviews, and consensus statements were considered. Given the narrative design, studies were selected based on relevance and methodological contribution rather than formal systematic screening.

Key content and findings

AI applications now span the full imaging-to-decision continuum, including image reconstruction, automated segmentation, quantitative assessment, phenotype recognition, and decision support. XR technologies enhance spatial understanding and pre-procedural planning, while computational modelling and three-dimensional (3D) printing enable patient-specific haemodynamic simulation and procedural rehearsal. Public datasets and integrated AI-XR-modelling pipelines are emerging. However, most evidence derives from feasibility and single-centre studies, and lesion-specific external validation remains limited.

Conclusions

AI, XR, and computational modelling hold significant promise for advancing cross-sectional imaging in CHD. Future progress will depend on multicentre collaboration, lesion-stratified validation, workflow integration, and governance frameworks tailored to lifelong congenital care. Demonstration of clinical outcome benefit will be essential for widespread adoption.

records.title: Deep learning prediction of MSI/dMMR, EBV, HER2, PD-L1, and CLDN18.2 status directly from hematoxylin and eosin-stained slides in gastric and gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma: a systematic review.

content.title: Deep learning prediction of MSI/dMMR, EBV, HER2, PD-L1, and CLDN18.2 status directly from hematoxylin and eosin-stained slides in gastric and gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma: a systematic review.
content.abstract:
Background

Microsatellite instability (MSI)/mismatch-repair deficiency (dMMR), Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2), programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1), and claudin 18 isoform 2 (CLDN18.2) are clinically relevant biomarkers in gastric and gastroesophageal junction (GEJ) adenocarcinoma, but molecular and immunohistochemical (IHC) testing is costly and not universally available. Deep learning (DL) applied to routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) slides may enable inexpensive pre-screening. We assessed the accuracy of DL models predicting these five biomarkers directly from H&E.

Methods

We searched PubMed, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, and Web of Science Core Collection from inception through 8 August 2026 for studies applying DL to H&E whole-slide or tissue-microarray images to predict MSI/dMMR, EBV, HER2, PD-L1, or CLDN18.2 status in gastric/GEJ adenocarcinoma. Two reviewers independently selected studies and re-extracted performance estimates from full texts, tables, footnotes, and supplementary materials. Risk of bias was assessed with Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 (QUADAS-2) and Prediction model Risk Of Bias ASsessment Tool (PROBAST) and certainty was assessed with Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE). Because the requirements for independent, variance-supported area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve (AUROC) estimates or threshold-specific 2 × 2 data were not met, study-level estimates were displayed without statistical pooling.

Results

Of 1,094 records identified, 701 unique records were screened and 28 studies were included: 18 addressed MSI/dMMR, 14 addressed EBV, 2 addressed HER2, 2 addressed PD-L1, and 1 addressed CLDN18.2; marker categories overlapped. External-independent AUROCs were 0.767 (95% CI, 0.726-0.830) for MSI/dMMR, 0.941 (0.920-0.970) and 0.859 (0.823-0.919) for EBV, and 0.856 (0.775-0.926) for CLDN18.2; broader held-out AUROCs were 0.760 and 0.880 (MSI/dMMR) and 0.980 (EBV). One report each provided eligible 2 × 2 data for EBV, MSI/dMMR, and CLDN18.2; none did for HER2 or PD-L1. No pooling or final-model calibration was supported. All 28 reports (42 analytic scopes) were high risk under PROBAST; QUADAS-2 risk was high for 40 scopes and unclear for 2. Certainty was very low for MSI/dMMR, EBV, HER2, and PD-L1 and low for CLDN18.2.

Conclusion

Individual held-out models sometimes showed promising discrimination, particularly for EBV and MSI/dMMR, but the evidence was too sparse, dependent, and heterogeneous to define a stable summary performance or a clinically deployable triage threshold. Certainty was very low for MSI/dMMR, EBV, HER2, and PD-L1 and low for CLDN18.2; clinical utility and calibrated threshold performance remain unestablished.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/, identifier CRD420261449992.

records.title: Efficacy and safety of chimeric antigen receptor T-cell in the treatment of hematologic malignancy: an umbrella review of systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Efficacy and safety of chimeric antigen receptor T-cell in the treatment of hematologic malignancy: an umbrella review of systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

This umbrella review consolidates data from systematic reviews and meta-analyses on the efficacy and safety of Chimeric Antigen Receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy in hematologic malignancies. The aim is to assess CAR-T efficacy across different malignancies, identify key safety concerns, and provide clinical recommendations.

Methods

We conducted a thorough search of PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews up to May 2024. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses evaluating CAR-T efficacy in hematologic malignancies were included. The AMSTAR tool was used to assess methodological quality, and the GRADE system was employed to evaluate the quality of evidence for each outcome.

Results

A total of 105 meta-analyses met the inclusion criteria. CD19-targeted CAR-T therapies demonstrated superior efficacy in acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), particularly in relapsed or refractory cases (high-quality). However, CAR-T monotherapy showed reduced efficacy in central nervous system lymphoma (CNSL) (middle-quality). Combination therapies, particularly CAR-T with HSCT, improved complete response rates but were associated with increased severe adverse events, such as CRS and neurotoxicity (high-quality). Axi-cel was found to carry a higher risk of ICANS and neutropenia compared to Tisa-ce (high-quality), likely due to its CD28 costimulatory domains, which enhance T-cell activation.

Conclusions

CAR-T therapy demonstrates promising clinical outcomes in ALL and DLBCL, but significant safety concerns remain. Combining CAR-T with therapies such as HSCT improves efficacy but also heightens the risk of severe toxicities. Future research should focus on optimizing CAR-T constructs, refining preconditioning regimens, and identifying predictive biomarkers to personalize treatment and mitigate risks in vulnerable populations.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/, identifier CRD42024581782.

records.title: Comparative efficacy and safety of fexuprazan versus esomeprazole in gastroesophageal reflux disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Comparative efficacy and safety of fexuprazan versus esomeprazole in gastroesophageal reflux disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

Fexuprazan is a newly emerging potassium-competitive acid blocker (P-CAB) medication. P-CAB drugs have been introduced as alternative medications for gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) instead of traditionally used proton-pump inhibitors (PPIs).

Aim

This study aims to compare the efficacy and safety of fexuprazan in contrast to esomeprazole.

Methods

An electronic search was conducted on major databases, and retrieved results were subjected to two stages of filtration based upon a preset inclusion criterion. The first stage filtered articles based on their titles and abstracts, and the second stage filtered articles based on their full texts. Articles found fit to include in this study were extracted using a pre-set piloted extraction form. Extraction results were introduced into a spreadsheet. Data was divided into categorical and numerical data. Categorical data was reported as counts and frequencies, while continuous data was reported as proportions, means, and standard deviations. Common and random effect meta-analyses were conducted as found fit. Risk of bias assessment was performed using the Cochrane's risk of bias assessment (RoB 2.0) tool.

Results

Five articles were included in the present review, describing 965 patients managed with fexuprazan 40 mg or esomeprazole 40 mg for a mean of 9.6 weeks. The mean age of patients was 50.2 ± 13.0 years. GERD symptom scores showed a numerically lower value in the fexuprazan group (SMD - 0.41 [95% CI: -1.10; 0.29], p = 0.25), though this difference was not statistically significant and the confidence interval crosses the null (I 2 = 94.5%, p < 0.01). The proportion of patients reporting symptom improvement did not differ significantly between groups (RR 0.85 [95% CI: 0.6; 1.22], p = 0.39; I 2 = 91.3%, p < 0.01). No significant difference was observed in the incidence of treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs; RR 1.07 [95% CI: 0.9; 1.27], p = 0.45; I 2 = 0.0%) or adverse drug reactions (ADRs; RR 1.10 [95% CI: 0.79; 1.53], p = 0.59; I 2 = 0.0%).

Conclusion

No statistically significant difference in efficacy was identified between fexuprazan and esomeprazole; however, preliminary findings are consistent with non-inferiority. No statistically significant difference in the incidence of TEAEs or ADRs was observed between treatments, suggesting a comparable safety profile.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261286108.

records.title: Efficacy and safety of goniotomy and gonioscopy-assisted transluminal trabeculotomy for exfoliation glaucoma: a systematic review and single-arm meta-analysis.

content.title: Efficacy and safety of goniotomy and gonioscopy-assisted transluminal trabeculotomy for exfoliation glaucoma: a systematic review and single-arm meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Objective

To assess the efficacy and safety of goniotomy (GT) and gonioscopy-assisted transluminal trabeculotomy (GATT) with or without phacoemulsification (PEI) for exfoliation glaucoma (XFG).

Methods

Searches were conducted in PubMed, Scopus, Embase, Ovid, and the Web of Science. Two independent reviewers performed study selection, data extraction, and quality assessment. The primary outcomes were the reduction in intraocular pressure (IOP) and the number of antiglaucoma medications (AGMs) at 1, 6, and 12 months postoperatively. Safety was assessed by the incidence of complications.

Results

Fourteen studies involving 624 eyes were included. The GATT ± PEI group showed significant IOP reductions of 1.96 mmHg (p < 0.01), 2.17 mmHg (p < 0.001), and 2.07 mmHg (p < 0.001) at 1, 6, and 12 months, respectively, with corresponding AGM reductions of 3.28 (p < 0.001), 2.87 (p = 0.003), and 2.54 (p = 0.011). The GT + PEI group demonstrated IOP reductions of 1.95 (p < 0.001), 2.00 (p = 0.040), and 2.13 mmHg (p = 0.013), with AGM reductions of 1.07, 0.96, and 0.96 (all p < 0.001). For standalone procedures, GT significantly reduced AGMs at all timepoints (all p < 0.001) and IOP at 1 and 6 months (both p = 0.002), while standalone GATT significantly reduced IOP only at 1 month (2.39 mmHg, p < 0.001) and AGMs at 6 and 12 months (both p < 0.001). The most common complications were anterior chamber hemorrhage (47.6%) and IOP spike (17.0%).

Conclusion

This meta-analysis demonstrates that GT and GATT, particularly when combined with phacoemulsification, are safe and effective in reducing IOP and medication burden in patients with XFG. The evidence for sustained IOP lowering with standalone GATT remains limited, suggesting that combined surgery may offer more reliable long-term pressure control, especially for patients with concurrent cataract.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/display_record.php?ID=CRD420251072295, identifier CRD420251072295.

records.title: Simulator development using natural language: clinician-led innovation through artificial intelligence.

content.title: Simulator development using natural language: clinician-led innovation through artificial intelligence.
content.abstract:
Background

Healthcare simulation training faces significant barriers due to the "clinician-developer gap," where educators lack programming expertise to create customized digital simulators. Natural Language-Driven Development (NLDD) is an emerging paradigm that enables clinicians to develop educational technology through conversational artificial intelligence interfaces.

Methods

We implemented NLDD methodology to develop Open Vent Sim, a comprehensive mechanical ventilation simulator designed to replace anesthesia machines and ventilators in educational contexts lacking dedicated equipment. A multidisciplinary team comprising anesthesiologists, residents, a research nurse, IT, and biomedical engineers collaborated using Google AI Studio to iteratively create a web-based application through natural language prompts. Development proceeded through conversational cycles in which clinical requirements were translated into functional code via large language model assistance.

Results

Open Vent Sim was successfully developed in about 40 h over two weeks, featuring three simulation environments: anesthesia workstation, ICU ventilator, and high-flow oxygenation systems. The simulator incorporates physiological patient profiles (normal, ARDS, COPD) with dynamic compliance calculations and realistic waveform generation. Clinical validation was achieved through the integration of continuous resident feedback during iterative development. The application was successfully implemented in SimZone 1 as an interactive skill trainer and in SimZone 2 for team-based clinical scenarios during formal anesthesia and critical care education. Significant technical adaptation was required to transform the AI-generated prototype into a production-ready application.

Conclusions

NLDD demonstrates the potential to democratize the creation of educational technology by empowering clinical domain experts to develop sophisticated simulation tools without traditional programming expertise. This approach addresses resource limitations while maintaining clinical authenticity, though professional technical oversight remains essential for production-ready implementations.

records.title: Performance of artificial intelligence models for predicting intraoperative complications during surgery in real time: a systematic review and meta-analysis protocol.

content.title: Performance of artificial intelligence models for predicting intraoperative complications during surgery in real time: a systematic review and meta-analysis protocol.
content.abstract:
Introduction

Intraoperative complications contribute significantly to morbidity and mortality, and reducing their risk is a primary objective for all operating room's healthcare professionals. Many of these complications are predictable and could be anticipated by the surgeon or anaesthesiologist. Various clinical scores were developed to assess cardiovascular risk, acute kidney injury or acute respiratory failure preoperatively. However, these scores require time for calculation and are not designed to be adjusted in real time during surgery, based on physiological signals and new intraoperative events. Besides, some events remain unpredictable because they are multifactorial.In recent decades, Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based algorithms have been tested for the real-time prediction of intraoperative complications. These algorithms have the potential to continuously analyse patient data and provide early warnings, enabling professionals to intervene more effectively.The aim of this review is to address the question: 'What is the performance of AI models in predicting intraoperative complications during surgery using baseline and real-time data?'.

Methods and analysis

The review will follow the Transparent Reporting of multivariable prediction models for Individual Prognosis or Diagnosis: Checklist for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses and BMJ guidelines. MEDLINE, Embase, CENTRAL (Cochrane), IEEE Xplore and Google Scholar databases will be explored for peer-reviewed papers up to 25 March 2025. First, two reviewers will independently screen titles, abstracts and full texts based on the inclusion and exclusion criteria. A third reviewer will resolve any disagreements. Eligibility criteria include AI models that predict or forecast intraoperative complications or immediate postoperative complications (up to the stay in the Post-Anaesthesia Care Unit) involving any patient undergoing surgery or interventional procedures with general or locoregional anaesthesia. The primary target is the algorithm's performance, depending on the choice of the authors. Key items from the CHARMS 2014 checklist will be extracted using a standardised form. Risk of bias assessment will be performed using the PROBAST+AI tool. If possible, meta-analysis will be conducted by implementing a random effects meta-analysis model.

Ethics and dissemination

Ethical approval is not required. The results will be published in a peer-reviewed journal and presented at national and international conferences.

Trial registration number

PROSPERO registration number: CRD420250599920. Any future amendments will be updated in the PROSPERO record.

records.title: Effectiveness of the GI Genius Computer-Aided Detection System Versus Standard Colonoscopy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.

content.title: Effectiveness of the GI Genius Computer-Aided Detection System Versus Standard Colonoscopy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
content.abstract: Colorectal cancer prevention relies on high-quality colonoscopy, yet clinically relevant lesions are still missed. GI Genius is an FDA-cleared computer-aided detection (CADe) system that flags suspected polyps in real time. We conducted a Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA)-aligned systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials in adults comparing GI Genius-assisted versus standard colonoscopy. PubMed, Ovid Embase, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) were searched from the earliest available records in each database through August 25, 2025, with citation chasing. Seven trials (n = 9,639) met the eligibility criteria. Random-effects meta-analyses showed that GI Genius increased the adenoma detection rate (ADR) compared with standard colonoscopy (RR 1.12, 95% CI 1.03-1.22; I²=64%). Secondary outcomes also favored GI Genius: polyp detection rate (PDR; two trials, n = 5,225; RR 1.05, 95% CI 1.01-1.10; I² = 0%), sessile serrated lesion detection rate (SSLDR; four trials, n = 7,013; RR 1.27, 95% CI 1.11-1.47; I² = 11%), and lesion counts (adenomas per colonoscopy/mean adenomas per patient, six trials, n = 9,253; standardized mean difference (SMD) 0.15, 95% CI 0.09-0.20; I² = 29%; polyps per colonoscopy/mean polyps, two trials, n = 5,228; SMD 0.10, 95% CI 0.05-0.15; I² = 0%). Advanced ADR (three trials, n=6,328) showed no significant difference (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.90-1.13; I² = 6%). Safety reporting was limited and was not included in the meta-analysis. In summary, adjunctive GI Genius improves clinically meaningful detection, increasing ADR, PDR, SSLDR, and per-procedure lesion counts, without a detectable effect on advanced adenoma detection. These findings support routine activation of GI Genius during eligible colonoscopies, contingent on appropriate team training and consistent response to system prompts. Larger multicenter trials with standardized methods and long-term clinical endpoints are warranted.

records.title: Diagnostic performance of deep learning for predicting glioma isocitrate dehydrogenase and 1p/19q co-deletion in MRI: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Diagnostic performance of deep learning for predicting glioma isocitrate dehydrogenase and 1p/19q co-deletion in MRI: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Objectives

We aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of deep learning (DL)-based radiomics models for the noninvasive prediction of isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) mutation and 1p/19q co-deletion status in glioma patients using MRI sequences, and to identify methodological factors influencing accuracy and generalizability.

Materials and methods

Following PRISMA guidelines, we systematically searched major databases (PubMed, Scopus, Embase, Web of Science, and Google Scholar) up to March 2025, screening studies that utilized DL to predict IDH and 1p/19q co-deletion status from MRI data. We assessed study quality and risk of bias using the Radiomics Quality Score and the QUADAS-2 tool. Our meta-analysis employed a bivariate model to compute pooled sensitivity and specificity, and meta-regression to assess interstudy heterogeneity.

Results

Among the 1517 unique publications, 104 were included in the qualitative synthesis, and 72 underwent meta-analysis. Pooled estimates for IDH prediction in test cohorts yielded a sensitivity of 0.80 (95% CI: 0.77-0.83) and specificity of 0.85 (95% CI: 0.81-0.87). For 1p/19q co-deletion, sensitivity was 0.75 (95% CI: 0.65-0.82) and specificity was 0.82 (95% CI: 0.75-0.88). Meta-regression identified the tumor segmentation method and the extent of DL integration into the radiomics pipeline as significant contributors to interstudy variability.

Conclusion

Although DL models demonstrate strong potential for noninvasive molecular classification of gliomas, clinical translation requires several critical steps: harmonization of multi-center MRI data using techniques such as histogram matching and DL-based style transfer; adoption of standardized and automated segmentation protocols; extensive multi-center external validation; and prospective clinical validation.

Key points

Question Can DL based radiomics using routine MRI noninvasively predict IDH mutation and 1p/19q co-deletion status in gliomas, and what factors affect diagnostic accuracy? Findings Meta-analysis showed 80% sensitivity and 85% specificity for predicting IDH mutation, and 75% sensitivity and 82% specificity for 1p/19q co-deletion status. Clinical relevance MRI-based DL models demonstrate clinically useful accuracy for noninvasive glioma molecular classification, but data harmonization, standardized automated segmentation, and rigorous multi-center external validation are essential for clinical adoption.

records.title: Comparative effectiveness and dose-response relationship of exercise-based interventions for muscle mass in older women with sarcopenia: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.

content.title: Comparative effectiveness and dose-response relationship of exercise-based interventions for muscle mass in older women with sarcopenia: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

Exercise and nutrition are the principal non-pharmacological strategies for sarcopenia, but the relative effects of different exercise combinations and the dose required to improve muscle mass in older women remain uncertain. This study compared exercise-based interventions and examined the dose-response relationship.

Methods

PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and EBSCO were searched from inception to 1 July 2026. Eligible trials enrolled women aged ≥ 60 years female with sarcopenia. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2. A frequentist random-effects network meta-analysis combined direct and indirect evidence, with effects expressed as standardized mean differences (SMDs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Interventions were ranked using P-scores. Network meta-regression examined control condition, age, intervention duration, weekly frequency, weekly exercise dose, and female proportion. A Bayesian model-based network meta-analysis assessed the dose-response relationship using MET-min/week.

Results

Twenty-seven controlled trials involving 1,845 participants were included. Heterogeneity was moderate, with no significant global inconsistency. Most interventions improved muscle mass compared with control, although no significant effect was detected for Chinese traditional exercise. Resistance, aerobic, and balance training combined with nutritional supplementation produced the largest effect (SMD = 1.41, 95% CI 0.81-2.01) and ranked first (P-score = 0.882). Control condition, age, and weekly exercise dose were significant effect modifiers, but covariate adjustment did not materially alter the intervention rankings. The dose-response relationship was positive and nonlinear. Within the central evidence-supported range, the lower 95% credible limit first exceeded zero at 460 MET-min/week (SMD = 0.19, 95% CrI 0.01-0.37). At the upper boundary of this range (1,144 MET-min/week), the predicted SMD was 1.38 (95% CrI 1.08-1.61).

Conclusion

Resistance-based multicomponent exercise may improve muscle mass in older women with sarcopenia, particularly when combined with nutritional supplementation. Exercise dose should be increased gradually according to individual tolerance. The reported dose values should be interpreted as evidence-supported estimates rather than fixed biological thresholds or universally optimal prescriptions.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261449654, identifier: PROSPERO (CRD420261449654).

records.title: The diagnostic value of artificial intelligence-assisted imaging for developmental dysplasia of the hip: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
records.publisher: Journal of orthopaedic surgery and research

content.title: The diagnostic value of artificial intelligence-assisted imaging for developmental dysplasia of the hip: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Objective

To clarify the efficacy of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted imaging in the diagnosis of developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) through a meta-analysis.

Methods

Relevant literature on AI for early DDH diagnosis was searched in PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and The Cochrane Library databases until April 4, 2024. The Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies tool was used to assess the quality of included studies. Revman5.4 and StataSE-64 software were used to calculate the combined sensitivity, specificity, AUC value, and DOC value of AI-assisted imaging for DDH diagnosis.

Results

The meta-analysis included 13 studies (6 prospective and 7 retrospective) with 28 AI models and a total of 10,673 samples. The summary sensitivity, specificity, AUC value, and DOC value were 99.0% (95% CI: 97.0-100.0%), 94.0% (95% CI: 89.0-96.0%), 99.0% (95% CI: 98.0-100.0%), and 1342 (95% CI: 469-3842), respectively.

Conclusion

AI-assisted imaging demonstrates high diagnostic efficacy for DDH detection, improving the accuracy of early DDH imaging examination. More prospective studies are needed to further confirm the value of AI-assisted imaging for early DDH diagnosis.

records.title: Artificial intelligence driven neuropsychiatry: a systematic review of electroencephalography-based computational techniques for major depressive disorder prediction.

content.title: Artificial intelligence driven neuropsychiatry: a systematic review of electroencephalography-based computational techniques for major depressive disorder prediction.
content.abstract: Major Depressive Disorder is the most prominent global mental health issue impacting millions of individuals worldwide. Electroencephalogram signals capturing intricate brain dynamics have emerged as a promising modality for predicting depression. This systematic review synthesizes research on computational techniques for depression prediction using neural signals, addressing the lack of standardized computational frameworks. The review identifies the significant variations in preprocessing pipelines such as bandpass filtering, artifact removal, and feature extraction techniques to assess their impact on predictive performance. A comparative analysis revealed significant variability in methodological approaches with deep learning architectures particularly convolutional neural networks and hybrid convolutional neural networks- Long Short-Term Memory models outperform traditional machine learning methods. Support Vector Machine also demonstrated competitive performance in several studies in terms of accuracy. Single channel and few-electrode configurations also show potential for cost-effective and portable diagnostic tools. Despite some studies reporting classification accuracies exceeding 90%, a lack of standardized evaluation protocols hinders the comparability of findings, representing a translational barrier for clinical adoption. This reflects a broader critical trend where methodological inconsistencies, data heterogeneity, and limited model interpretability hinder the generalizability and reliability of model. Future research should prioritize standardized protocols, diverse datasets, multimodal data integration, and explainable Artificial Intelligence to enhance clinical applicability. These insights provide a framework for artificial intelligence-driven electroencephalogram analysis to revolutionize depression diagnostics by guiding researchers to advance precision psychiatry through innovative and scalable solutions.

records.title: A systemic review of facial expression recognition (FER) in stroke: diagnosis and emerging applications in rehabilitation.

content.title: A systemic review of facial expression recognition (FER) in stroke: diagnosis and emerging applications in rehabilitation.
content.abstract:
Background

Stroke remains a leading cause of long-term disability and mortality worldwide, the early identification and evaluation of rehabilitation effectiveness are of great significance. Facial expression recognition (FER), a computer vision technology, offers potential for early screening and monitoring in many conditions. However, its application in stroke remains underexplored.

Aims

To offer insights into how the FER can be used in stroke identification and rehabilitation monitoring.

Methods

We systematically searched four databases, including PubMed, Web of Science, CNKI, and WanFang, for studies on FER applications in stroke, from database inception to January 2025.

Results

A total of 1,855 studies were identified, of which nine met the inclusion criteria (e.g., 8 diagnostic studies and 1 rehabilitation trial). Eight studies demonstrated FER's diagnostic utility for stroke, achieving accuracies ranging from 82 to 98% through facial asymmetry analysis during standardized tasks in public/private datasets. Specific tasks such as KISS, SPREAD, and non-speech movements were particularly effective. One study achieved 99.81% accuracy in monitoring rehabilitation intensity by classifying real-time facial expressions to tailor training intensity. The data sources included images (66.7%) and clinical patients database (55.6%).

Conclusion

FER technology exhibits substantial potential as an auxiliary tool in stroke diagnosis and emerging rehabilitation applications by enabling precise analysis of mandibular and facial movements. Nevertheless, FER models face considerable challenges in real-world clinical translation. Future research could integrate multimodal data and in-the-wild databases to facilitate the clinical implementation of FER technology, thereby improving care delivery for both patients and clinicians and reducing patient mortality and disability.

records.title: Risk factors for return to work in workers who experienced cancer: a systematic review with meta-analysis.

content.title: Risk factors for return to work in workers who experienced cancer: a systematic review with meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

The number of people who have experienced cancer is increasing, and by 2040 cases are expected to rise by 40%, with a high prevalence among working-age individuals. Many people who experienced cancer (pwEC) face reduced work ability due to health, personal, and occupational factors. Therefore, this study aims to identify the main factors that hinder RTW among pwEC.

Methods

A systematic literature search was conducted via PubMed, CINAHL, and the Cochrane Library, covering studies published between January 2012 and June 2024. Inclusion criteria focused on studies analysing RTW and Time to RTW in relation to sociodemographic, clinical, and occupational factors. Meta-analysis grouped studies by design, exposure, and effect measures. Fixed or random effects models were applied based on heterogeneity. Risk of bias was assessed using NOS and RoB2 tools. Certainty of evidence was assessed using GRADE tool and STROBE checklist.

Results

Among 2,151 screened articles, 43 met the inclusion criteria. Chemotherapy (OR = 0.56, 95% CI: 0.52-0.60) and radiotherapy were associated with a reduced likelihood of RTW. Women were more likely than men to RTW. Manual labour was linked to a lower likelihood of re-employment than white-collar jobs (OR = 0.84, 95% CI: 0.78-0.89). In terms of timing, male sex and chemotherapy delayed the process, whereas radiotherapy accelerated it (HR = 1.03, 95% CI: 1.00-1.06).

Conclusion

Identifying barriers to RTW after cancer is essential for improving quality of life and social reintegration in people who have experienced cancer. These findings highlight the complexity of RTW and the need for a personalized approach. However, the evidence is limited by heterogeneity and differences in study design.

Trial registration

The protocol was registered in PROSPERO (registration number: CRD42022384364).
